differences.title: 1. STORAGE MODEL
differences.leftDesc: TDengine organizes data around time-series primitives with efficient timestamp indexing and “super table” metadata. It persists columns per metric family while optimizing for common rollups and time-window scans.
differences.rightDesc: ClickHouse stores data in columnar parts (granules) with compressed encodings and vectorized execution. Queries typically read only needed columns, making scans fast for analytic workloads with wide tables.

differences.title: 2. INGESTION PATH
differences.leftDesc: TDengine is optimized for high-frequency IoT ingestion: it handles concurrent writes, partitions by time, and builds query-friendly structures during ingestion. It also supports automatic aggregation pipelines for fresh data.
differences.rightDesc: ClickHouse ingestion commonly uses INSERTs into tables backed by merging/partitioning logic. Near-real-time patterns rely on materialized views and background merges to keep data queryable quickly.

differences.title: 3. PARTITIONING & RETENTION
differences.leftDesc: TDengine partitions and organizes measurements by time ranges and metadata hierarchy, enabling targeted pruning. Retention and deletion can operate at granularity aligned with time partitions and automations.
differences.rightDesc: ClickHouse partitions tables by time (e.g., monthly/daily via Date partition keys) and manages lifecycle using ALTER TABLE DROP PARTITION or TTL expressions. This prunes data by partition and, optionally, row-level TTL.

differences.title: 4. AGGREGATIONS
differences.leftDesc: TDengine supports built-in time-series aggregation features that can continuously compute downsampled summaries. It maintains precomputed windows to accelerate queries over long time ranges with less CPU work at query time.
differences.rightDesc: ClickHouse accelerates rollups using materialized views and aggregated tables, plus specialized aggregate functions. It can compute aggregates during ingestion and serve them efficiently via grouping and pre-aggregation.

differences.title: 5. QUERY EXECUTION ENGINE
differences.leftDesc: TDengine’s execution is tuned for time-series patterns such as time-window predicates, tag-based filtering, and aligned aggregations. It minimizes unnecessary scans by leveraging its TS-aware metadata and indexes.
differences.rightDesc: ClickHouse uses a vectorized execution model with columnar operators, enabling SIMD-friendly processing and fast group-bys. The planner chooses pipelines and join/aggregation strategies optimized for high-throughput analytics.

differences.title: 6. HIGH CARDINALITY TAGS
differences.rightDesc: ClickHouse supports high-cardinality dimensions with careful table design, low-cardinality codecs, and effective partitioning. For tag-like filtering, it can push down predicates and read only required column data.
differences.leftDesc: TDengine’s super table model treats tags (like device attributes) as first-class metadata. It compresses and indexes tag values to reduce lookup overhead when filtering across many devices and metrics.

differences.title: 7. CLUSTERING & READ/WRITE SCALING
differences.leftDesc: TDengine provides a distributed architecture designed for time-series workloads where writes and time-based reads scale predictably. It focuses on partitioning by time and balancing metric families across nodes.
differences.rightDesc: ClickHouse scales horizontally via sharding and replication, using distributed tables to route inserts and queries. Consistency and performance depend on replication settings, partitioning, and background merge behavior.
